name: Sara Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Stonebridge, a goat farm with about two hundred milking goats, plus hay, lucerne for feed, and a big vegetable patch for the farm shop. Elena and Marco own it and make cheese. I'm in the milking parlour at six, then I clean down, then it's whatever's needed, hay in summer, kids in spring. Baby goats, I mean, not children, though they behave about the same.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two and a half years. Before that I worked twenty-seven years at a bank branch in town, behind the counter and then on mortgages. They closed the branch when everyone went to banking on their phones, and I took the redundancy money. I'm still learning, I'm slow at the hay baler and Marco has to check my cheese turning, but I like that every day I can see what I've done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, a lot of fuss about not much. I'd probably say it at the farm shop counter when people chat, because they always ask about the news. And I'd add that it's still worth learning a bit of it, because something always changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good news, really. I'd get to see out my last years at Stonebridge without another upheaval. I've already had one job vanish from under me, I'm not keen on a second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to check what's wrong with a goat before I bother Marco, and I'd keep doing that. Luca and I would keep saving, and we'd stick to the plan of me working to 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any part of you that doesn't quite believe it would stay this quiet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small one. When the bank first brought in the apps, everyone said it was a gimmick, old people won't use it. Five years later the branch was shut. So I'd be calm, but I'd keep one eye open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the bank teach you, would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That you don't wait for the letter. At the bank, the ones who'd quietly looked around were fine. The ones who said it'll never happen were in shock for months.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, a lot of fuss about not much, probably to customers at the farm shop counter. But I'd add it's still worth learning a bit, because something always changes.
S0.think: For me it's good news: I'd see out my last years at the goat farm without another upheaval. I've already had one job vanish from under me and I'm not keen on a second.
S0.do: Carries on as she is, using the phone AI now and then to check goat health before calling the owner. Keeps saving with her husband and sticks to the plan to work to 65.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly pleased, with one eye open.
S0.quote: When the bank first brought in the apps, everyone said it was a gimmick, old people won't use it. Five years later the branch was shut.
S0.fieldNote: Sara's bank career ending with a branch closure is her main reference point. Even in the mildest picture she remembers that the banking apps were once called a gimmick. Her lesson is simple: don't wait for the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like the banks, but on every street at once. Some of it's good, some of it's going to hurt people, and we should be sensible about it. I'm not one for shouting either way, I'd just say get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd expect a milking robot at Stonebridge in a few years, they exist already for goats. That's my mornings gone. But I've got savings, I've got options, and I've done this once before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I did at the bank, but earlier: look around before the letter comes. I'd ask Elena and Marco if I could help with the cheese and the shop more, because people still want to buy cheese from a person. I'd pick up the AI tools a bit more once I saw the others using them, and Luca and I would put a bit extra into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the weeks before the branch closure, when there were rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the farm do you think is safest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm shop, and the cheese tastings on Saturdays. People drive out from town to chat to us and taste the new batch. I can't see anyone driving half an hour to chat to a robot about goat cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you think it's time to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena would tell me, she's straight. I trust her more than I trusted the bank, where we found out from a memo. That's part of why I'd stay calm-ish.

S1.say: I'd say it's like the banks, but on every street at once. Some of it's good, some of it will hurt people, and we should be sensible and get ready.
S1.think: I'd expect a milking robot at the farm in a few years, since they exist for goats, and that's my mornings gone. But I've got savings and options and I've done this before.
S1.do: Looks around before any letter comes and asks the owners to move her onto cheese and shop work. Picks up AI tools a little more once colleagues use them, and adds to savings with her husband.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the weeks of rumours before the bank branch closed.
S1.quote: I can't see anyone driving half an hour to chat to a robot about goat cheese.
S1.fieldNote: She is pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, blaming no one and preparing early. She bets on the customer-facing side of the farm as the part machines won't take. Trust in the owners keeps her steadier than she was at the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments and businesses talking right now, not in a year. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it everywhere, at the shop and to friends. I'm not political, but two years is too fast for anybody to just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out by 60, and the cheese and shop might not save me. If everyone's out of work, who's buying artisan goat cheese? We'd be all right on savings. But it's my second job gone in five years, and I'd have nothing to move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd sit with Luca and work out stopping at 60. We'd keep spending normal but stop the extras, and move most of our savings into something steady. When it arrived, I'd leave Stonebridge when Elena needed me to, help my daughter if she needed it, and probably do the farm shop's books part time if they'd still have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the night we got the branch memo, but worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said at the bank you had time to look around. What does two years of warning take away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the chance to look around. With the bank, I had a year of rumours and I used it to plan. Two years for the whole world means no other job to move to, so all the looking around in the world doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Luca's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luca's an electrician. In the short run he'd be busy, wiring up all these robots, and he's said as much over dinner. Then the robots would do the wiring too. So maybe two good years and then the same as me.

S2.say: I'd say governments and businesses need to talk right now, not in a year. I'm not political, but two years is too fast for anybody to just shrug.
S2.think: I'd be out by 60, and the cheese might not save me, because if nobody's working, who's buying artisan goat cheese? We'd be fine on savings, but it's my second job gone in five years.
S2.do: Plans with her husband to stop work at 60, cuts extras and moves most savings into something steady. Leaves the farm when the owners need her to, helps her daughter if needed, and offers to keep the shop's books part time.
S2.feel: Anxious, like the night the branch closure memo came, but worse.
S2.quote: If everyone's out of work, who's buying artisan goat cheese?
S2.fieldNote: Her safe-ground theory from the slower picture collapses here, and she sees it herself. Money is secure, but losing a second job in five years stings. Her husband's trade gives two good years and then the same end, which she says without drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a bit of time, so let's be sensible and plan. I'd say employers should give long notice and governments should set up retraining money. And I'd tell my friends to stop pretending it won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be 63, so it's two years off my plan. Annoying, but not a disaster. I'd be uneasy rather than frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Stonebridge and move into the shop and cheese side over the next couple of years, as I'd planned anyway. I'd learn the AI tools properly, maybe a short course, because it'd make me more useful to Elena for the shop's orders and accounts. We'd keep saving and probably bring retirement forward to 63 and enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steadier. I could see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of course are you picturing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short evening one at the community college, they do 'AI for small businesses'. Marco's already asked me to look at it, to help with the online orders. Before, I'd have said I'll wait. With five years coming, I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this you'd find hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. The money's fine. But I liked the idea of going at 65, on my own terms. Being told when, twice in one life, is a lot.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a bit of time, so let's be sensible and plan, with long notice from employers and retraining money from government. And I'd tell friends to stop pretending it won't happen.
S3.think: I'd be 63, so it takes two years off my plan, which is annoying but not a disaster. I'd be uneasy rather than frightened.
S3.do: Moves into the farm's shop and cheese side over the next two years and takes an evening course on AI for small businesses to help with orders and accounts. Keeps saving and brings retirement forward to 63.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadier, because she can see a path.
S3.quote: Being told when, twice in one life, is a lot.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her into an earlier adopter than usual: she'd take the course she would otherwise put off. The money is secure; what bothers her is losing control of timing again. She remains pragmatic and blames no one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up, and people have no excuse not to prepare. I'd say it at the shop, nicely. Some of the younger ones would roll their eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired at 65 well before it lands. I'd be thinking about my daughter, Giulia, who's 31 and works in a hotel abroad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Stonebridge as normal, move toward the shop over time, and pick up the AI tools at my own pace. Keep our money plans the same and retire at 65. Talk to Giulia when she's home at Christmas about what she might do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little wistful for the farm as it is now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Giulia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That hotels will still need people for a good while, but not as many, and she should think about what she's best at with guests. She speaks three languages. Maybe that matters less with AI translating everything, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust it to really take ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly. I said that about phone banking too, and I was wrong then. So I'd plan as if it would.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up and people have no excuse not to prepare. I'd say it nicely at the shop, and the younger ones would roll their eyes.
S4.think: I'd be retired at 65 well before it lands. I'd be thinking about my daughter, who works in a hotel abroad.
S4.do: Carries on at the farm, shifts toward shop work and learns AI tools at her own pace. Keeps money plans and retirement at 65 the same, and talks with her daughter at Christmas about what she might do next.
S4.feel: Calm, with a little wistfulness for the farm as it is now.
S4.quote: She speaks three languages. Maybe that matters less with AI translating everything, I honestly don't know.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture lands after her retirement, so her attention moves to her daughter. She admits she doesn't know what will matter. Her bank experience makes her plan as if it will happen even while doubting it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be nowhere to move to. What would help is long notice from employers by law, say a year, and proper money for retraining, not a leaflet. At the bank we got a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people my age can still do. I came to goats at 55 after a career with spreadsheets. I'm slow and I'm learning, but I'm proof you can change. People shouldn't be written off at 58.

headlineQuote: At the bank we got a leaflet.
portrait: Sara Rossi is 58 and worked 27 years at a bank branch until it closed when customers moved to phone banking. For two and a half years she has worked at Stonebridge, a goat dairy with hay, lucerne and a farm shop, still learning the practical work. She is pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, uses AI tools now and then, and her rule is not to wait for the letter. In the slower pictures she plans a move toward the shop and cheese side, which she thinks machines won't take; in the two-year AGI picture she's anxious, seeing that even that would fail if nobody had work. She is financially secure, and what bothers her most is losing control of her timing a second time.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be nowhere to move to.
whatWouldHelp: A legal duty for employers to give long notice, around a year, and real money for retraining rather than a leaflet.
